cim: Local authorities warn of AI-powered scams ahead of the holidays
cim_eredeti: Local authorities warn of AI-powered scams ahead of the holidays
szoveg_eredeti:
TUCSON, Ariz. (13 News) - Scammers are using artificial intelligence to make their schemes more convincing, and local authorities are urging people to stay alert as the holidays approach.

One of the biggest warning signs is urgency: A caller or message may pressure someone to act immediately, without taking time to verify the request.

The Pima County Sheriff’s Department says scammers use social media to find potential victims and AI to create fake identities. Voice cloning can also make an impostor sound like someone the victim knows, including a family member supposedly facing an emergency.

Other schemes can involve fake lottery winnings, overpayments, business impersonation, romantic interests and demands to buy gold. Scammers can also disguise their phone numbers to make them appear local.

According to the FBI, Arizona ranked seventh in the nation for scam complaints in 2025, with reported losses of $631 million. The top three scam categories involved investments, tech support and confidence or romance scams. Arizona ranked fourth for complaints from people over 60.

Tyler Rivas, a detective with the Pima County Sheriff’s Department’s fraud unit, said seasonal residents can be targets.

“Southern Arizona is a hotbed for scams, especially for the older generation that come here for our great weather,” Rivas said. “Scammers know that when they see the increase on people that come here for the seasonal residence. It’s a target.”

Scams can affect people of any age. PCSD says younger people reported losing money to fraud more often than older people in 2025, but older victims may have more assets for scammers to target. In Pima County, PCSD says 27.7% of victims were over 60, nearly 4 percentage points above the national rate.

Authorities say warning signs include being pressured to keep a transaction secret, drain an account or buy cryptocurrency or gold. Scammers may also try to isolate a victim from people they trust.

FBI Supervisory Special Agent Gregory Clark said scammers may call and pretend to be a person’s bank, claiming there are suspicious purchases on the account. They can then use information the person provides to carry out a scam.

The FBI advises people to “take a beat” before responding. Authorities recommend:

Scammers may also impersonate the FBI. The agency will not demand payment or personal information through an unsolicited call, text or email. If someone claims to represent the FBI, verify the contact independently.

Anyone who suspects a scam can call the Pima County Sheriff’s Department fraud unit at 520-351-3000, even if they are unsure whether fraud occurred. A deputy can help assess the situation.

People can also contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324) or through its official contact page.

Authorities encourage victims to come forward, even if they feel embarrassed. If you have sent money, report it promptly; law enforcement may be able to help you try to recover lost funds, although recovery is not guaranteed. PCSD says it can be harder to retrieve money sent outside the country.
